findings.message: When EnableGzipCompression is true and compression throws any non-cancellation exception, the catch block swallows the error, sets isCompressed=false, and proceeds to send uncompressed content. PublishAsync then returns Result.Success(). The caller (orchestrator) has no indication the message was not compressed as configured. Receivers built to always expect Content-Encoding: gzip from this endpoint will fail to decode messages that were silently sent uncompressed, with no error surfaced to the operator.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: the catch block at lines 144-149 swallows non-cancellation exceptions from compression, sets isCompressed=false, and proceeds to send uncompressed content with no Content-Encoding header, returning Result.Success(). Receivers expecting Content-Encoding: gzip will silently receive uncompressed payloads with no error surfaced to the caller.
findings.severity_justification: Causes a silent contract violation — receivers built to always decompress gzip will fail to process the message, but the impact is limited since compression failure on an in-memory GZipStream is very rare in practice. The lack of error surfacing is the main concern.
findings.category_justification: The issue is about error handling and graceful degradation: a configuration expectation (compression) is silently violated without propagating the failure to the caller or operator.

findings.message: The validator iterates ApplicationProperties.Keys and checks for reserved or whitespace keys, but never validates values. A null value (e.g. from JSON 'key': null, or programmatic null! assignment) will pass validation and reach CreateMessage where it is written as message.ApplicationProperties[key] = null (cast to object). The Azure Service Bus AMQP encoder does not support null application property values and will throw at send time, producing a runtime failure that bypasses the normal Result failure path.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The core impact claim — that Azure Service Bus AMQP encoder throws on null application property values — is unverifiable from available context and is likely incorrect since AMQP protocol natively supports null typed values. The `Dictionary<string, string>` type with NRTs enabled also nominally prevents null values at compile time, limiting the real exposure.
findings.severity_justification: Even if null values somehow bypassed NRT annotations via JSON deserialization, AMQP supports null in application properties and the SDK likely handles them gracefully rather than throwing.
findings.category_justification: The concern is about missing input validation that could cause runtime failures.

findings.message: Inside the retry while-loop, client.CreateSender(entityName) creates a new ServiceBusSender on every attempt but the sender is never disposed. ServiceBusSender implements IAsyncDisposable and holds an AMQP link. On each transient retry, the previous sender's link is leaked until the ServiceBusClient is eventually disposed. This is pre-existing but the PR adds a retry path that is now exercised more frequently when compression is enabled and a transient failure occurs.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: client.CreateSender(entityName) is called inside the while loop at line 158 with no using/await using disposal. On each transient retry the sender is abandoned undisposed. This is confirmed pre-existing from git history (present before this PR). The finding is factually correct about the leak.
findings.severity_justification: ServiceBusSender AMQP links are lazy-initialized and the retry count default is 3, limiting exposure. The client's DisposeAsync eventually cleans up. The PR doesn't materially worsen this.
findings.category_justification: Resource leak — ServiceBusSender implements IAsyncDisposable and should be disposed after use.

findings.message: ApplicationProperties is typed as Dictionary<string, string>. Azure Service Bus ApplicationProperties natively supports typed values (bool, int, long, double, DateTimeOffset, Guid, Uri, etc.); receivers can retrieve these as strongly-typed objects via ApplicationProperties[key] as int. By restricting to string values, the feature forces receivers to parse strings where they may expect typed values, and makes it impossible to configure typed metadata (e.g. a priority integer or a boolean flag) through this configuration mechanism.
findings.tp_fp_justification: While factually correct that Azure SB supports typed application properties and the config is restricted to string, Dictionary<string,string> is the standard and expected type for configuration-driven properties since all config sources (appsettings.json, env vars) are string-based. The finding states a general API design preference without demonstrating a concrete broken use case or a precedent in this codebase for typed config values.
findings.severity_justification: Even if addressed, supporting typed config properties would require significant schema complexity and string parsing is a common pattern for config-driven metadata.
findings.category_justification: The concern is about the type design of a configuration property and its impact on callers/receivers of the API.

findings.message: The new ServiceBus validation block reuses the same seenNames HashSet that was already populated by the Local and Sftp loops. This means a ServiceBus destination whose name matches any existing Local or Sftp destination name will now fail startup validation with 'Name X is duplicated.' Any deployment with cross-type name reuse (previously allowed since ServiceBus was not validated) will begin failing at startup after this change with no migration path other than renaming.
findings.tp_fp_justification: While factually correct that seenNames is shared across all three type loops, the finding incorrectly frames this as problematic. The SimpleFileRouter.ResolveKind() resolves destinations by checking Local→Sftp→ServiceBus in order, so any deployment with cross-type name sharing would already have broken routing (ServiceBus destination unreachable). The validator correctly enforces cross-type uniqueness that was semantically required but previously unenforced.
findings.severity_justification: Any deployment affected by this validation change would already have been experiencing silent routing bugs, so the validation failure is surfacing an existing misconfiguration.
findings.category_justification: The finding concerns whether the validation logic correctly captures semantic constraints of the system.

findings.message: The comment says runtime properties 'can override configured ones if keys collide', implying that configured and runtime property keys can collide at runtime. In fact the validator uses OrdinalIgnoreCase to reject all reserved keys at startup, making the described collision impossible under normal operation. However the case-sensitive Dictionary at runtime does not enforce this: if validation is bypassed (e.g. in tests or future code paths), a configured key like 'fh.FILEID' and the runtime key 'fh.fileId' will both be present as distinct entries in the dictionary, sending both to Service Bus consumers.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: the runtime Dictionary<string,string>() is case-sensitive (default Ordinal comparer) while the validator's ReservedApplicationPropertyKeys uses OrdinalIgnoreCase. The comment 'can override configured ones if keys collide' is inaccurate under normal operation since validation prevents the collision. A case-variant reserved key bypassing validation would coexist as a distinct entry rather than being overridden.
findings.severity_justification: The inconsistency only manifests if validation is bypassed (e.g. in tests or direct construction). In production with the validator running, reserved keys are blocked OrdinalIgnoreCase so the gap is theoretical.
findings.category_justification: The finding identifies a factual inaccuracy in a comment plus a real case-sensitivity inconsistency between validation and runtime behavior.

findings.message: DecompressAsync is a public static method included in the production library but has no call site in production code—it is only used by tests. Dead public API in a production assembly signals to consumers that server-side decompression happens here, which it does not; decompression is a receiver concern. Additionally, DecompressAsync handles corrupted input by letting GZipStream throw InvalidDataException unguarded, which callers may not anticipate for a method that has no documentation about exception behavior.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: DecompressAsync has zero call sites in src/ production code — only used in test/. It is a public static method in a production assembly with no production purpose. The finding is factually correct about the dead API.
findings.severity_justification: Dead code in an application assembly (not a published library) is a maintainability concern but has no runtime impact. The unguarded exception concern is minor since callers in tests handle it fine.
findings.category_justification: Dead public API with no production call site is a code cleanliness/maintainability issue.

findings.message: The GZipStream in CompressAsync is instantiated with leaveOpen: true, but the underlying MemoryStream is not flushed before ToArray() is called. GZipStream buffers data and writes a footer upon disposal. Because leaveOpen is true, disposing the GZipStream doesn't dispose the MemoryStream, but it does flush the final compressed data to it. The current code disposes GZipStream *after* calling ToArray(), resulting in a truncated or empty byte array being returned.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The finding's core claim is factually wrong about execution order. The await using block disposes gzipStream (flushing buffer and gzip footer to outputStream) before the closing brace, and outputStream.ToArray() is called after that. The code is correct — leaveOpen:true keeps outputStream accessible after gzip disposal, and the full compressed data including footer is captured by ToArray().
findings.severity_justification: If the finding were correct it would be a critical data corruption bug, but it is factually wrong so severity applies to the incorrect claim itself.
findings.category_justification: The finding claims incorrect behavior about compression output truncation.

findings.message: The runtime properties `fh.fileId` and `fh.protocol` can override custom properties defined in the configuration if they use the same keys. The validator prevents this for new configurations, but this behavior could be unexpected. Runtime-generated properties should be added without overwriting existing keys, or a warning should be logged if an override occurs.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The validator's ReservedApplicationPropertyKeys (OrdinalIgnoreCase) explicitly blocks fh.fileId and fh.protocol from being configured, preventing the override scenario under normal operation. The finding acknowledges this and the remaining concern is a design preference for defensive coding. The suggested fix (don't overwrite existing keys) would actually produce wrong behavior if validation were bypassed by silently sending incorrect runtime property values.
findings.severity_justification: The scenario requires validation to be bypassed and the suggested fix would be semantically incorrect, making this a non-actionable preference.
findings.category_justification: The finding is essentially a defensive coding style suggestion rather than identifying a concrete bug.

findings.message: When logging a successful publish, `LogPublishSuccess` is called with `attempt`, which is the retry attempt number. For a successful first try, `attempt` will be 0, which may be confusing. The attempt counter should be incremented before logging to be 1-based, or the log message should be clarified.
findings.tp_fp_justification: LogPublishSuccess already handles attempt=0 correctly via an explicit else branch that logs at Debug without showing attempt count. The attempt+1 math in the if-branch correctly computes total attempts for retry successes. The suggested fix (increment before logging) would break the logic by making first-try success log 'after 2 attempts'.
findings.severity_justification: The code is correct; the finding is based on a misreading of the conditional logic in LogPublishSuccess.
findings.category_justification: The finding makes a claim about incorrect logging behavior that is factually wrong.

findings.message: The test `Validate_ServiceBusDestination_WithValidConfig_Succeeds` does not validate any `Storage` destinations. The validator's logic iterates through both `Storage` and `ServiceBus` destinations, but this test and others in the file only cover `ServiceBus`, leaving the `Storage` validation logic untested in this new test file.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The finding claims the validator iterates through 'Storage' destinations, but no such type exists in DestinationsOptions or DestinationsOptionsValidator. The validator only iterates Local, Sftp, and ServiceBus collections. The finding is factually incorrect about the codebase.
findings.severity_justification: The finding is entirely fabricated — there is no Storage destination type to test.
findings.category_justification: The finding is about missing test coverage for a non-existent code path.

findings.message: The only publisher-level test added for gzip compression is skipped, so the new path that compresses the message body and sets `Content-Encoding` is not exercised by the automated test suite. Please add an active unit test (for example by extracting/mocking message creation) so regressions in the Service Bus publishing behavior are caught without requiring a live Service Bus.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified in the file: `Compression_Enabled_Publishes_Compressed_Content` is decorated with `[Fact(Skip = "Requires live Service Bus or refactoring for mock client")]`. The publisher path that calls `CompressionHelper.CompressAsync`, sets `isCompressed`, and writes `Content-Encoding: gzip` to message application properties is therefore never executed in CI. The finding is factually correct and identifies a concrete gap in automated test coverage for newly introduced behavior.
findings.severity_justification: The compression utility itself is tested in `CompressionHelperTests`, and the skipped test has an explicit explanation. The gap is real but not high-risk — it's a missing integration-style test for a clearly bounded feature, and the compression logic is already unit-tested separately.
findings.category_justification: The finding is specifically about a skipped test leaving new publisher behavior unexercised by the automated test suite.

findings.message: This XML documentation uses a raw `<` character, which makes the doc comment invalid XML if documentation generation is enabled. Escape it as `<` so generated API docs remain well-formed.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified in the file: line 49 (`/// Note: Small messages (< 1KB) may become larger...`) contains a raw `<` character inside the `<remarks>` XML doc block, outside any `<code>` element. This is invalid XML and will cause doc-generation tools (e.g., DocFX, Sandcastle, or `dotnet doc`) to warn or produce malformed output. The `<` should be escaped as `<`.
findings.severity_justification: Affects only documentation generation output, not runtime behavior. The compiler will typically produce an XML comment warning (CS1570) but still compile successfully.
findings.category_justification: The issue is with an XML doc comment producing malformed XML when documentation is generated.

findings.message: This newly requires every Service Bus destination to include credentials, but the existing service registration explicitly supports a no-auth configuration by registering `DisabledFileContentPublisher` when no destination has a connection string or namespace (`src/FileHorizon.Application/ServiceCollectionExtensions.cs:170-174`). With this validation, those configurations now fail as soon as `DestinationsOptions` is resolved instead of using the disabled publisher path.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: the ServiceCollectionExtensions.cs publisher factory explicitly supports a no-credential fallback to DisabledFileContentPublisher. The new validator added by this PR fails validation for any ServiceBus destination lacking both ConnectionString and FullyQualifiedNamespace. Because CurrentValue triggers IValidateOptions before the credential check runs, configurations that previously fell through to the disabled publisher now throw OptionsValidationException instead.
findings.severity_justification: Could break existing deployments or dev/test configurations that rely on configuring ServiceBus destinations without credentials to get no-op publishing behavior. Startup would fail with OptionsValidationException instead of silently using the disabled publisher.
findings.category_justification: The new validation logic conflicts with a pre-existing intentional code path, changing observable startup behavior for configurations that previously worked.
